title: Engineering topological phenomena via field-driven Weyl motion
abstract: We illustrate the field-driven anomalous Hall engineering via the momentum-space motion of Weyl nodes using pyrochlore iridates under a [111] magnetic field as an example. We model the system with a well-established microscopic Hamiltonian and the field effect with the spin rotation from the all-in-all-out to the ferromagnetic state. Tracking the position of Weyl nodes during the spin rotation, we demonstrate macroscopic anomalous Hall conductivity variations are fundamentally driven by Weyl node motions by comparing the full multi-band Kubo formula with the geometric Weyl node separation. The discrepancy occurs only near a critical spin rotation angle, where several Weyl nodes come into close proximity. We reveal that the evolution of anomalous Hall conductivity under the magnetic field agrees with reported experiments in an order-of-magnitude and non-monotonicity. These results elucidate the field-driven dynamics of momentum-space monopoles and provide a framework for understanding transport in strongly correlated topological materials.
summary: This work theoretically models how changing the magnetic order in pyrochlore iridates drives topological phenomena, specifically the motion of Weyl nodes. By comparing the Kubo formula to geometric node separation, the authors demonstrate that the resulting anomalous Hall conductivity is fundamentally controlled by these momentum-space monopoles. This provides a quantitative framework for predicting transport properties in strongly correlated topological insulators.
main_problem: The paper investigates how the anomalous Hall conductivity (AHC) in topological materials is engineered by the field-driven motion of Weyl nodes in momentum space.
main_result: The computed intrinsic AHC exhibits non-monotonic behavior and shows an order-of-magnitude agreement with experiments, confirming that Weyl node dynamics fundamentally drive the transport properties.
method: The authors compare two theoretical calculations for AHC—the full multi-band Kubo formula and the geometric Weyl node separation—by tracking node movement as the magnetic state changes.
model_or_system: The system studied is pyrochlore iridates, modeled using a microscopic Hubbard Hamiltonian that is treated within a mean-field approximation. The magnetic state is varied by simulating the spin rotation from an antiferromagnetic (AIAO) to a ferromagnetic (FM) state under an external magnetic field.
key_observables: Anomalous Hall Conductivity (AHC), Weyl node positions, Berry curvature flux, and the discrepancy between Kubo and node-separation calculations.
important_parameters: The magnetic canting angle $\theta$ (ranging from $109.47^\circ$ to $0^\circ$), the external magnetic field direction ([111]), and the critical angle $\theta_c \approx 14^\circ$.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the Hartree-Fock mean-field approximation for the Hubbard interaction and assumes the magnitude of local moments remains fixed during spin rotation.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the crystal structure, the Hamiltonian components (hopping terms), the spin rotation path, and the band structure evolution, highlighting the Weyl nodes in k-space.
paper_structure: The paper builds the Hamiltonian using a tight-binding model incorporating hopping terms and a mean-field magnetic exchange term. It then calculates AHC using both the Kubo formula and the geometric node separation method, analyzing the resulting dependence on the magnetic canting angle $\theta$.
why_interesting: The explicit connection drawn between the Berry curvature flux (a topological invariant) and measurable transport coefficients like AHC provides a powerful theoretical framework for understanding topological materials, which is relevant to understanding exotic quantum states in correlated systems.
